(p-140) Surah At-Tariq (The Night-Comer)

Makkan, and its verses are seventeen.

﴿By the sky and the Tariq.﴾ Al-Tariq (the Night-Comer) is originally an active participle from ṭaraqa, ṭarqan and ṭarqan, meaning he came at night. Al-Mawardi said: The root meaning of ṭarq is knocking (al-daqq), and from it the mallet (al-mitraqah) is named. The one who arrives at night is called ṭāriq only because he generally needs to knock on the door. Then the term was extended to everything that appears at night, whatever it may be, and this extension was pushed further until it was applied to the phantom images that appear visibly at night. He said:

"A phantom came at night, not like a traveller by night, whose footsteps were heard by us and who did not display himself."

What is meant here is the star that appears at night, either as a generic noun or as a specific, well-known star. It has also been said: al-Tariq is the star that is called the Morning Star (kawkab al-subh).

The saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And what will make you know what the one that knocks is?﴾ serves to draw attention to its (the matter's) importance, after its magnification by swearing an oath by it, and it is an alert that the elevation of its rank is such that the perception of creation cannot attain it, so it must be received from the Creator, the All-Knowing. So "mā" (what) the first is a subject (mubtada') and "adrāka" (made you know) is its predicate, and the second is a predicate, and "al-ṭāriq" (the one that knocks) is a subject, as has been explained in its parallels. That is: "And what thing made you know what the one that knocks is?"

Translation:

And His saying, ﴿the piercing star﴾, is the predicate of a deleted subject, and the sentence is a resumption (istinaf) that came as an answer to a question arising from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" So it was said: "The star that is brilliant to the utmost degree, as if it pierces the darkness or the celestial spheres with its light and penetrates them. What is meant by it is either the genus, for every star has a piercing light without doubt; or a specific known star. It was said: it is Saturn (Zuhal). It was said: it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). It was said: it is the Pole Star (al-Jadi). It was said: the piercing star is a star in the seventh heaven which no other inhabits; when the stars take their places in the sky, it descends and is with them, then it returns to its place in the seventh heaven, which is Saturn, so it is a visitor (tariq) when it descends and when it ascends. As for its mention, when swearing by it, with a description shared between it and other things, then the pointing out that this description is not the true reality of its matter, and that this is among the things that human thoughts cannot reach, and then its explanation as the piercing star, from the magnifying of its affair and the exalting of its station, is evident."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 86, verse 4:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is over every soul a guardian﴾ is the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam), and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) brought for what has been mentioned of emphasizing the grandeur of the one sworn by, which entails emphasizing the content of the sentence sworn to. "In" is negative (nafiyah), and "lamma" is in the sense of "illa" (except). That is: there is not every soul except that over it is a guardian (hafiz), watcher (muhaymin), observer (raqib), and He is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is ever over all things an Observer﴾. It has been said: he is the one who preserves its deeds and records against it what it earns of good and evil, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ ﴿noble, recording﴾, the verse, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him﴾. And it has been read "lamma" with a light pronunciation (mukhaffafah), on the basis that "in" is a lightened form of the heavy (thaqilah) "inna", whose noun, which is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), is omitted, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqah), and "ma" is an additional particle (za'idah), meaning: indeed the matter is that every soul, over it is surely a guardian.

The fāʾ in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾ serves to draw attention to the fact that what has been explained, namely that over every soul there is a guardian who records for it everything that proceeds from it of speech and deed, makes it incumbent upon man to reflect deeply upon the origin of his creation, until it becomes clear to him that He who was able to bring him into being from substances that had never tasted the scent of life at all is able to bring him back, and indeed more able by the measure of reason. Thus he will act, for the Day of Return and of Recompense, in a way that benefits him and profits him on that day, and will not dictate to his recording guardian anything by which he would be refuted.

This is a translation of the passage as given. Note that the passage ends mid-sentence, at the asterisk, and I have translated it exactly as it stands.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Created from a gushing fluid﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that came as an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "From what was he created?" So it was said: "He was created from a fluid that gushes (dafiq)," and this is what is poured forth, having propulsion and flowing with speed. What is meant by it is the mixture of the two fluids in the womb, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates, *

It emerges from between the loins and the ribs. That is: the loins (sulb) of the man and the ribs (tara'ib) of the woman, which are the bones of her chest. They say: the semen (nutfah) is generated from the surplus of the fourth digestion (al-hadm al-rabi') and separates from all the organs, until it becomes prepared that similar organs may be generated from it. Its seat is a set of veins, some of which are intertwined with others, near the two testicles. The brain is the greatest of the organs in assisting its generation, and for this reason it resembles it; excessive intercourse causes weakness in it. It has a substitute, which is the spinal cord (al-nukha'), and it lies in the loins, and it has many branches descending to the ribs. These two (the loins and the ribs) are closer to the vessels of the seminal fluid (al-mani), and for this reason they were singled out for mention. It has been read as "al-salab" with two fathas and "al-sulub" with two dammas, and in it there is a fourth dialect, "salib."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 86, verse 8:

﴿Indeed He﴾: the pronoun refers to the Creator, Exalted is He, for His saying "created" (khuliqa) points to Him. That is, He who created him originally from what has been mentioned.

﴿is able to return him﴾: that is, to bring him back (i'adah) after his death.

﴿to be Most Capable﴾: clearly able (la-bayyin al-qudrah), meaning His power is manifest and beyond doubt.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 86, verse 9:

﴿On the Day when the secrets are tested﴾. That is: what is concealed in the hearts of beliefs and intentions and other things is made known and examined, and what was hidden of deeds is scrutinized, and what is good among them is distinguished from what is corrupt. And it (p-142)

is an adverbial complement (zarf) governing "rajʿihi" (His returning him).

﴿So he will have﴾, i.e., the human being, ﴿no power﴾ in himself by which he can defend himself,

﴿nor any helper﴾ by whom he may be aided.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 86, verse 11:

﴿By the sky, which returns⁠﴾ (﴿وَالسَّمَاءِ ذَاتِ الرَّجْعِ﴾). That is, the rain. It was called "return" (raj'), because the Arabs used to claim that the clouds carry water from the seas of the earth and then return it to the earth. Or they intended by this an omen (tafa'ul) that it would return (liyarji'a). For this reason they also called it awb (return). Or because God Most High returns it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And the earth, which splits open﴾ refers to what the earth splits open with of vegetation (al-nabat). Or it is a verbal noun (masdar) from the passive form (al-mabni li-l-maf'ul), meaning its being split open by vegetation, not by springs (al-'uyun), as has been said. For the description of the heaven and the earth when swearing by them points to the truth of the Qur'an, which speaks of resurrection (al-ba'th), through the two qualities mentioned. This is to indicate that both of them, in themselves, are among its evidences. This is the secret in the expression of "splitting" (al-sad') regarding it, and "returning" (al-raj') regarding rain. That refers to the earth's splitting open with vegetation, which imitates resurrection (al-nushur), as mentioned in several places in the revelation (al-tanzil), not to its splitting open with springs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 86, verse 13:

﴿Indeed, it﴾ i.e., the Qur'an, of which what has been recited of the verses that speak of the origin of man's state and his return (ma'ad) is a part.

﴿is indeed a decisive word﴾ i.e., one that separates truth from falsehood, and this is an intensified description, as though it were the very essence of decisiveness (fasl).

Qur'an 86:14: ﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ There is no trace of jest in any part of it; rather, all of it is pure seriousness, with no leniency in it. Therefore it is fitting that the misguided be guided by it and that the necks of the obstinate tyrants submit to it.

Translation:

﴿Indeed they﴾: that is, the people of Makkah.

﴿are plotting﴾ to nullify his affair and extinguish his light.

﴿a plot﴾, in accordance with what it denies them the power to do.

I will translate the passage as instructed.

﴿And I will plot a plot﴾, meaning: I will confront them with a firm scheme that cannot be repelled, whereby I lead them on gradually (istidraj) from where they do not know.

﴿So give the disbelievers respite﴾. That is, do not occupy yourself with taking vengeance on them, and do not call down destruction upon them, or do not hasten it. The *fa'* (فَ) indicates that what follows it is a consequence of what precedes it, since the report that He, the Exalted, Himself takes charge of their scheming is by itself something that necessitates granting them respite and refraining from confronting them in their plotting, definitively.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Give them respite﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "*mahhil*" (مَهِّلْ). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿gently (*ruwaydan*)﴾ is either an emphatic infinitive (*masdar mu'akkid*) reinforcing the meaning of the verb, or an adjective (*na't*) qualifying its omitted infinitive, so that the sense is: "Give them respite, a gentle respite (*imhalan ruwaydan*)," meaning "nearby," as Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, or "a little," as Qatadah said.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: "It is originally the diminutive of *rud* (رُودٍ) with a damma, and he recited:

*"As if she were a drunkard walking slowly on her rud."*

That is, "at a leisurely pace." It has also been said that it is a diminutive of *rawwad* (رَوّادٌ), a verbal noun of *rawd* (رَوْدٌ), with apocope (*tarkhim*). In usage it has two other forms: that it is a verb-like particle (*ism fi'l*), as in "*ruwaydan Zayd*" (take it easy, Zayd), and that it is an adverbial accusative of state (*hal*), as in "*sara al-qawmu ruwaydan*" (the people walked slowly), meaning "moving leisurely." In expressing the substitute with a form that does not allow for multiplicity, and in restricting it with "*ruwaydan*" according to one of the two mentioned possibilities, there is an evident consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a calming of his heart.

It is also related from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Tariq, Allah will grant him ten good deeds for every star in the sky." And Allah knows best.
